# Transcript Formatting - Thematic Sections - v12-Lite

## Section 1 – Gratitude at Billy's Grave ([00:03:00]).

Billy, thank you for allowing me to grow up. I went to the cemetery where my mother and father are buried, and in a different place just by the cemetery, I went to his grave. I stood over his grave and I said, "Billy, thank you for allowing me to grow up."

## Section 2 – Introduction to Michael Kerr and Bowen Theory ([00:33:00]).

The man you just heard is Michael Kerr. For more than 60 years, Bowen theory has been part of his life, first as Murray Bowen's student and later as one of the people who carried his work forward. This conversation is not simply about a psychological theory. It is about what happens when someone spends a lifetime applying that theory to his own family, his marriage, his clinical work, and eventually to the society around him.

What follows is Michael Kerr's perspective on Bowen theory, told through the experiences that shaped his understanding of it and the ideas that can help us understand our own families, relationships, and the systems we live in. The family requires understanding by using systems thinking, which was different from Freudian thinking. In the 1950s, one influential idea in psychiatry blamed schizophrenia largely on the mother, the so-called "schizophrenogenic mother." Murray Bowen took a different approach. At the National Institute of Mental Health, he began observing patients together with their families. What he saw led him away from explanations focused on one individual and toward the family as an emotional system.

## Section 3 – Discovering Bowen in Medical School ([01:44:00]).

If I hadn't had this lucky break of hearing him give a lecture when I was in medical school, the thing that caught my ear was: this guy is not blaming the mother, he's blaming the whole family. We're all involved in this. And that was a real wake-up call for me. I was just damn lucky to run across him and then to be around him and with him for the next 12, 15 years or so.

**Michael Kerr:** Sure. Well said.

## Section 5 – Trees and Connectedness in Living Systems ([04:30:00]).

In his book, Michael draws on Peter Wohlleben's work on forests to illustrate a central idea: no living organism exists entirely on its own. Trees are connected, they exchange resources, and they respond to one another. I asked him why he chose this image for a book about human relationships.

**Michael Kerr:** It's just trying to recognize the connectedness of every form of life on the planet. People with birds, birds with people, and so on through the whole living world. The family requires understanding by using systems thinking, which was different from Freudian thinking.

## Section 6 – The Family as an Emotional System ([05:29:00]).

Bowen saw the family not as a collection of separate individuals, but as an emotional system. What one person feels and does does not stay with that person. It moves through the relationships and changes the system around them.

**Interviewer:** You describe the family as an emotional system.

**Michael Kerr:** Birds have an emotional system. Every living thing on the planet has an emotional system.

In Bowen's theory, anxiety does not affect every member of a family in the same way. Sometimes one child becomes the focus of the family's worry, protection, and emotional intensity. Bowen called this the family projection process. For Michael, that idea was deeply personal.

## Section 7 – Personal Example: Billy as the Focused Child ([06:27:00]).

This is a picture of me and my four brothers. I'm the youngest there on the floor. My brother Billy would be on the right side of the photograph, and he was the one eventually diagnosed with schizophrenia. I think that gave me an opening, when I first heard Bowen, to recognize that this guy really understands interactions in families and how they work. When he was born, my mother thought he was a fragile china doll who needed much protection. And she really believed that. I stood over his grave and I said, "Billy, thank you for allowing me to grow up." Something like that. I think the whole thing was a powerful experience because he was the one who took the bigger force of the family system, whereas my brother Terry and Bob and myself got off the hook. So I thanked him. It seemed an important thing to do. And I was lucky enough, as I said, to have a brother who took the weight off me. A big deal. I thanked him for it. I really meant it. Years later, she said to me, "Michael, I love you, but I love Billy the most." I said, "Thank you."

## Section 9 – Chronic Anxiety as the Invisible Force ([09:15:00]).

**Michael Kerr:** What we see is that most people drift to blaming or self-blaming, and they can't see that, like Bowen described, it is anxiety that is flooding through the system, going from one person to the other, and everyone is reacting to it. Yeah. I'm right in the midst of a manuscript that can explain chronic anxiety as opposed to acute anxiety. It gives information on what generates this chronic anxiety, which is more imagined than real. Acute anxiety is usually more real, and chronic anxiety is more not understood. I think, to escape the family process, it is necessary to understand how this chronic anxiety develops.

**Interviewer:** Acute anxiety being real threats, chronic anxiety being imagined threats for the most part.

**Michael Kerr:** That was Bowen's way of saying it.

**Interviewer:** Do you think that this chronic anxiety is having its own life within the system, and it's like an invisible enemy that nobody can see but everyone is reacting to it?

**Michael Kerr:** Yeah, that's a good way to say it. Yeah. To realize that what's driving this is chronic anxiety, and to understand that, and understand your part in generating that chronic anxiety. That's the pathway to change. You first have to see it differently than you ever saw it before.

**Interviewer:** But this emotional reactivity is feeding the invisible enemy, isn't it?

**Michael Kerr:** Right. Chronic anxiety, and what that really is to the world around us. Like turning on the news at night now, everything is trauma, trauma, trauma. And it doesn't get anybody anywhere until, as I said earlier, we become forced to do something.

## Section 10 – Chronic Anxiety and Inflammation ([12:18:00]).

I think chronic anxiety can generate chronic inflammation that you're not really all that aware of, and can be the undergrowth for all kinds of physiological problems and diseases. That's, I think, chronic inflammation being different from chronic anxiety, or chronic anxiety driving chronic inflammation.

One of the writers I was reading said it's time clinicians and researchers in psychology and physiology take it seriously. You can't call it something psychosomatic, but in the end, it's somatic. It's not psychosomatic, it's somatic. A very useful idea, I think. Brain states that produce mental illness also activate inflammation, and again, psychological stress, more and more I think, is being appreciated as activating inflammation and predicting later psychopathology.

## Section 11 – Self-Differentiation ([13:47:00]).

In Bowen's theory, the concept of self-differentiation means that you're not fused into the emotional system, so that you can learn that your feelings are not your thoughts and that you don't have to react to what's coming up in your body. Self-differentiation is on a scale. We have no self, pseudo-self, and solid self. And what Murray Bowen was saying is that most people are operating on the pseudo-self, which means that they are not themselves. They are wearing masks, they are fitting into the system, and they are reacting to the anxiety that is flooding through the system. Here's a quote. It's a little long, but I'll read it because it's a quote from Murray Bowen: "Operationally, ideal family treatment begins when one can find a family leader with the courage to define self, who is as invested in the welfare of the family as himself; who is neither angry nor dogmatic; whose energy goes to changing self rather than telling others what they should do; who can modify self in response to the strengths of the group; and who is not influenced by the irresponsible opinions of others. When the family member moves toward differentiation, the family symptoms disappear. A family leader automatically generates mature leadership qualities in the other family members who are to follow." I forget where that is in his book, but somebody I know sent that to me. I think this is probably one of the best quotes he ever had. So what Murray Bowen is saying with that quote is that a family needs a mature leader who takes responsibility for the welfare of the family and also invests his energy into self-differentiation. That's a hard job to do, isn't it? A lot of responsibilities for one person.

## Section 12 – No Technique, Only Self-Change ([16:30:00]).

Notice what is not in that paragraph. No technique, no confrontation, no telling anyone else what to do. The energy goes into changing self. Bowen's claim is striking: when one person becomes more differentiated, the functioning of the whole family can begin to shift.

## Section 14 – Steps Toward Self-Differentiation ([19:16:00]).

**Interviewer:** What can one do when he or she realizes, "Oh, I'm acting on my pseudo-self. I want to become more my solid self"? What's the first step to take, besides analyzing the system? What can one do to become more mature?

It's all you need to do. Time, time, time. Having kids that we were raising really gave me a kick in the ass when they hit teenage stuff. That offered us, thanks to Bowen theory and my interactions with him, the ability to see again this idea of an interaction you never could see before. But if you can do that, then you're on the road to being able to change the way you respond.

## Section 16 – Learning Neutrality from Murray Bowen ([21:22:00]).

When I first got supervised by Murray Bowen, my mother and schizophrenic brother were in the Philadelphia area, and I was heading home for a visit. When I got back, the Monday or Tuesday after I got back from the weekend, I met with Murray Bowen and I started to spill out what had happened over the weekend. Then I looked up at him, and he hadn't said much of anything, and I said, "He's smiling. What's he smiling about?" But then I realized he hadn't got tangled up with it, with me. And that was a big step to help me start doing something differently. It was the first time I had seen that he could stay outside the system with my utterings and utterings and utterings. And that was very helpful itself, having the therapist really be neutral because of his own experience of doing that.

**Interviewer:** I think it's much easier to stay out of an emotional system that is not yours than in your family?

**Michael Kerr:** When you worked with people who told their stories, it was much easier to have a neutral stance than when interacting with your mother or other extended family, wasn't it?

**Interviewer:** Absolutely. And I mean, what I can say from experience is that you know exactly when they poke you. You know exactly what comes along, and then your emotions jump over. You're reacting without even noticing it, and two seconds later it's like, "Oh, I fell into that trap again."

## Section 17 – Continuous Learning Through Bowen Theory ([23:30:00]).

**Michael Kerr:** Yeah. I think about what's – I've been involved in Bowen theory, what, 60 years now - I guess, I can still learn to see things that I never saw before by having this body of knowledge. Study it. Study your part in it.

## Section 18 – Entry Point: Multigenerational Perspective ([24:30:00]).

**Interviewer:** Let's say someone stumbles across Bowen theory and reads about it, and this person says, "Okay, I want to see it in the system. I want to analyze the system and my role in it." Where can he or she start exploring his or her family? What's the best entry point?

**Michael Kerr:** Getting that multigenerational perspective is extremely important, and not blaming your parents or your grandparents. When people get a perspective on this, that any one person is not creating this problem, it's an interactive process that's creating the problem, it allows them to make progress when they see that. Some people have a much harder time seeing that than others. And certainly people in more dire straits in society have a harder time doing that as well. That's not their fault. This is part of a multigenerational process.

## Section 19 – Distance Is Not Differentiation ([25:54:00]).

When a family becomes unbearable, distance can feel like freedom. You move away, call less, go quiet. Bowen described this pattern as emotional cutoff. But distance, in his theory, is not the same as differentiation.

**Michael Kerr:** When I told Mother that I was going to go into psychiatry based on my exposure to Bowen, she said to me, "Michael, I thought you were going to be a doctor." And it sort of took me aback, but it was very helpful to see that in the long run. She wanted me, in her heart of hearts, to finish my training, come home, move in with her and my schizophrenic brother, and spend the rest of our lives playing this out. That wasn't for me. I spent two years in the Navy after finishing my psychiatric rotation, and by then I had been working with Murray Bowen for a few years. I think I sent him a letter about six months into my time in the Navy. I was out at Great Lakes Naval Hospital. He sent me a letter saying, "Mike, if this is how you deal with your family, no wonder you had so much trouble."

**Interviewer:** So he was judging you for running away?

**Michael Kerr:** Yeah. Right, right, right. For leaving the system. That was not his idea, leaving the system. You have to heal in the system.

**Interviewer:** Exactly. That's the most complicated part of his theory: healing in the system, or differentiating while in the system. You can't run away from yourself and from that system. I think that's what people have to realize, that leaving the family and running away is not solving the problem.

**Michael Kerr:** Bingo.

## Section 20 – Physical Distance Versus Differentiation ([28:59:00]).

One distinction matters here. Physical distance and differentiation are not the same thing. Distance can change the setting. Differentiation changes how you function in relation to the system. It means staying grounded in your own position without automatically being pulled into its emotional reactivity. And that is different from remaining in contact when contact is unsafe.

**Michael Kerr:** The contact with Bowen changed my whole life. I'd probably be divorced by now, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, if I hadn't had this lucky break of hearing him give a lecture when I was in medical school. I was just damn lucky to run across him, and then taking on the responsibility after he died to try to fill his shoes. That wasn't easy.

**Interviewer:** But you did great. I mean, you added neurobiology and biology to the theory. You showed that emotional fusion leads to illnesses, that the body is reacting to it. So you did a great job.

**Michael Kerr:** Well, thank you.

## Section 21 – Societal Regression ([30:29:00]).

In Bowen's theory, societal regression describes what happens when chronic anxiety spreads through an entire society. As anxiety rises, people and institutions become more reactive, more polarized, and more focused on immediate relief than long-term consequences. In that sense, a society can begin to function much like an anxious family system.

**Interviewer:** You worked with Bowen, and in 1975 he said that emotional reactivity spreads beyond the family system into institutions, communities, even entire societies. He called it societal regression, and he was criticized for it a lot. Can you explain what societal regression looks like, and what are signs that it is happening?

**Michael Kerr:** Well, the easy way to say it would be: turn on the television. Listen to the news all over the world. These are signs of societal regression, but nobody has caught on to that idea outside Bowen theory. I read in one of the books of your colleagues, she was elaborating on societal regression, and she said that in the early '90s we saw in the statistics that divorce rates were going up, youth criminality at a high point. So there were certain indicators that it had already started, and that was about 15 years after Bowen stated this is something that is happening. And now we are 35 years later. Like you said, chronic anxiety is coming into your living room each evening.

**Interviewer:** Yeah, it's hard to believe how regressed the world is, but there it is.

**Michael Kerr:** How is this trend affecting people, particularly individuals with a higher level of self-differentiation?

**Interviewer:** Well, they're going to be less drawn into the finger-pointing and blaming. But look around the world at world leaders. Authoritarianism is popular. Anyway, that's a big question. I'm not sure what to say.
